newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajikistan's fragile peace a hostage to gunmen.
newsitem.headline: Tajikistan's fragile peace a hostage to gunmen.

text.p: Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov appears to have wriggled out of a tight corner once more. But peace remains a hostage to the myriad armed groups that call the shots in this former Soviet republic on the border with Afghanistan.

Only weeks after the embattled Tajik leader buried the hatchet with Islamic opposition guerrillas -- signing a peace deal in June to end four years of civil war -- weekend clashes between two warlords supposedly loyal to Rakhmonov threatened his enfeebled presidency with collapse.
A third warlord, Makhmud Khudoyberdyev, a mutinous colonel commanding an elite armoured brigade in the south, seized on the chaos in Dushanbe and moved his tanks towards the capital.
Having mutinied twice before and wrung concessions out of Rakhmonov, the colonel no doubt thought a third show of force would win him some more.

After fighting with pro-Rakhmonov forces for four days, however, the once powerful colonel has apparently limped back to barracks and accepted Wednesday's dismissal from his command by Rakhmonov without a whimper.
Rakhmonov kept his head down throughout the crisis but by firing the renegade commander, the former boss of a collective farm seems to have shown finally some political backbone.
But as with most crises in the chronically unstable republic of 5.7 million which borders Afghanistan, there are more questions than answers as to why fighting erupted.
The rebel colonel's own motives remain shrouded in mystery and there has been no word from him since his dismissal.
Khudoyberdyev, who fought the guerrillas, has been open about his opposition to peace with the Islamists and reluctant to see 500 of their number return to Dushanbe as agreed under the peace accord.
He used the issue to declare autonomy for his southwestern region around Kurgan Tyube last month, setting up a "Defence Council" to run it -- deemed "unconstitutional" by Dushanbe.
Observers say the 34-year-old colonel has long term political ambitions.

But it is unclear whether Khudoyberdyev was intent on a full-blown military coup or if he was caught off guard by Rakhmonov's armed response to a move which might only have been intended as more muscle-flexing.
Whatever the reason, he appears to have miscalculated.
The colonel lost control of an aluminium smelter, one of the republic's few sources of cash, and -- if the government is to be believed -- the brigade upon which his power was based.
As the dust settles, 45-year-old Rakhmonov remains weak and dependent on several private armies which have subjected the mountainous country to gun law similar to that in Afghanistan.
Their rockets and grenade launchers might put violin-case carrying mobsters in the shade but the weekend fighting in Dushanbe was essentially a mafia-style battle for turf.
The winner, the commander of an armed interior ministry unit called Sukhrob Kasimov, is sure to lean on Rakhmonov after aiding his presidential guard in fighting the colonel.

"Rakhmonov's fairly safe in his position because nobody wants his job," said a Western diplomat in Dushanbe. "Much better to be a supporter so you get to run your rackets without having to worry about bothersome affairs of state".
Russia, with 20,000 of its own troops in the republic which guard Tajikistan's frontiers and carry out peacekeeping duties, stayed well in the background throughout the crisis.

Rakhmonov is heavily dependent on the Kremlin for backing of his shaky administration. Russia made its presence felt during the unrest by puting up armed posts around the city under the guise of peacekeepers deployed by the Commonwealth of Independent States.
"Rakhmonov's problem is how to move the country from a neo-feudal clan system to strong government and some sort of national unity," the diplomat said.
But with the economy in tatters after the civil war and a gun the easiest way of making money, Tajikistan is a long way from the peace and stability most of its inhabitants so desperately crave.
